articles.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Will Be Easier to Platinum Than Rebirth
articles.summary: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is still a few months away, but it seems like it's at least going to be easier to get the Platinum trophy than it was in Rebirth.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is still a few months away, but it seems like it's at least going to be easier to get the Platinum trophy than it was in Rebirth.

Speaking to Anime News Network , game director Naoki Hamaguchi was asked why only 2.6% of PS5 players had the Platinum trophy for Rebirth, specifically citing the post-game VR boss gauntlets and the perfect play they required. And while Hamaguchi stands by the design decisions, he does explain why the trophy was so out of reach.

"For Rebirth's platinum trophy — well, for Rebirth in general — there's so much to do. There's so much content. We wanted to make people go through all this content and perfect it. It's kind of by design that that would make it difficult." Despite that difficulty, Hamaguchi doesn't regret making it that way, saying, "So, I don't want to call it a mistake in judgment or anything, but we also didn't expect so many people to want the platinum trophy. I think that was what we underestimated here. Battle director Teruki Endo also saw [the fan reaction] and was like, 'Oh, no! I feel bad — I have regrets.'"

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Preview Screenshots

While the Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Platinum trophy will probably still be huge in scope, it should at least be a little bit easier to get, especially where the superbosses are concerned. "In comparison, for Revelation, the platinum trophy will be easier to get," Hamaguchi says. "In terms of how difficult it will be, we're expecting twenty percent of players or maybe even more than that to be able to obtain it." Specifically, he mentioned that, "It's not just about the amount of battles that there are, but the battles themselves that are going to be enjoyable. I think that's one thing that we've learned from Rebirth: to make the battles themselves enjoyable rather than just challenging."

It sounds like the optional bosses aren't going to be quite as much of a grind as they were in Rebirth, though hopefully there is still some challenge there.

We won't have to wait too much longer to see how these post-game battles play out. Final Fantasy Revelation comes out on February 8, 2027 for Xbox Series X, PlayStation 5, PC and Nintendo Switch 2. And while you will need to download it to play, even if you buy it on a disc , you can at least expect the game to last for more than 100 hours.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: The 8BitDo Ultimate 2C Is One of the Best PC Gaming Controllers and It Only Costs $24
articles.summary: Compatible with Windows PC, Android, and Steam Deck.
articles.body:
You don't need to pay $150, $100, or even $50 for an excellent PC gaming controller. The 8BitDo Ultimate 2C Wireless PC Gaming Controller is already attractively priced at $29.99 and is arguably the best controller at that price point. However, ahead of Prime Day, Amazon has dropped the price by another 20% to $23.99. Only lavender is discounted, but I own this exact model and color way and I have to say it looks great in person. I really like this controller and recommend it to anyone who doesn't want to spend $80 or more on a Gamesir G7 Pro (my other favorite controller).

8BitDo Ultimate 2C Wireless Controller (Switch Compatible)

8BitDo Ultimate 2C Wireless PC Gaming Controller

The 8BitDo Ultimate 2C is a wireless PC controller that has a lot of premium features you wouldn't expect in a sub-$30 controller. Running down the list, the controller itself feels solid with no rattle and a pleasant grippy matte texture. Both the joysticks and triggers use magnetic Hall Effect switches, which means no moving parts to wear out and no stick drift to contend with. Not even high end controllers like the PlayStation DualSense Edge or the Xbox Elite have Hall Effect switches. The joysticks in particular are also reinforced with metal rings for extra durability.

The Ultimate 2C has extra R4/L4 bumpers that can be custom mapped without needing to download any resource hogging softwarel. Other features include a convenient Turbo button and immersive rumble vibration. The Ultimate 2C supports Bluetooth but a USB dongle is also included that allows for a stable 2.4GHz wireless connection with 1,000Hz polling rate.

Note that this controller is compatible with Windows and Steam PCs and mobile devices (via Bluetooth). It is a perfect controller for your handheld gaming PC like the Steam Deck, ASUS ROG Ally (including Xbox Ally), and Legion Go.

articles.title: The Next Fourth Wing Book Releases Next Week — Here's Where to Buy
articles.body:
Rebecca Yarros' Empyrean Series is getting a new addition next week. Threshing Day is set to arrive on September 29.

Yarros announced the new title earlier this year and preorders for the book have been dominating Amazon's best-seller charts since then. Unlike the first three novels in the series, Threshing Day is a collection of short stories detailing the day various characters bonded with their dragons. If you're hoping to pick up a copy as soon as possible, here's the rundown of where to buy and which formats are available.

Threshing Day (Wing and Claw Collection)

There is only one hardcover version of the book releasing on September 29 and it's part of the Wing and Claw collection. That just means it features the stencilled edges other new releases have all gotten.

If you're hoping to pick up a hardcover copy for the lowest possible price, Amazon is the way to go. As the biggest online bookstore in the world, they almost always offer the best deal . Target had also matched that lower price, but preorders have already sold out there ahead of release. The only potential issue with preordering from Amazon is that you won't actually get the book until October. So if you want your copy before then, your best bet is to order a full-price version at Barnes & Noble for in-store pickup.

If you'd prefer a normal hardcover edition of the book, you'll have to wait a bit longer. Barnes & Noble and Target are the only stores currently offering preorders for this version and it isn't getting released until October 13.

If you prefer to listen to your favorite romantasy series in audiobook form, the good news is the audio version of the book is releasing at the same time as everything else. The overall best deal on the audiobook is at Amazon where you can preorder it for $14.39. You can also get it for free when you sign up for a free trial of an Audible subscription .

There are actually two different audiobooks releasing for this book at different times, the first being of the standard narration variety. If you prefer full-cast audiobooks instead, you can wait for the GraphicAudio version arriving on October 13. Both are eligible for Audible credits or a free trial of the service.

The full cast list has not yet been announced, but we already have an idea of what to expect based on previous GraphicAudio releases of Fourth Wing. In addition to multiple voice actors, the audio experience will include music and sound effects.

For those who prefer to read via their Kindle devices , Threshing Day is also releasing an eBook version on September 29. Other than the audiobook version, this is the quickest way to get access to the book as soon as it releases. You can preorder the book directly from the Kindle Store for $11.99 ahead of its release.

Jacob Kienlen is a Senior Audience Development Strategist and Writer for IGN. Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, he has considered the Northwest his home for his entire life. With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics — from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets .

articles.summary: EA Sports FC 27 reviewed by Andrew McMahon on PS5 Pro, also available on PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC."EA Sports FC 27 is a game caught between two competing directions. The revamped passing and crossing, deeper Career Mode systems, and greater emphasis on strategy give more meaningful control and reflect the improvements that help build on the series’ strongest foundations. At the same time, those improvements are repeatedly undermined by inconsistent CPU behavior, lingering defensive issues, technical problems, slow menus, and an open-world hub that is disconnected from what fans want from a virtual soccer experience. So while the soccer itself is enjoyable, the series is still searching for the right balance between innovation and making the core game work the way it should."

articles.title: EA Sports FC 27 Review – The Grounds is Shaky, But the Tactics System Shows Promise
articles.summary: EA Sports stands on shaky ground with a new open-world hub, but the realistic, intuitive Tactics system shows promise.
articles.body:
I find myself in a weird place with EA Sports FC 27. On one hand, worthwhile strategic elements have finally been added that reflect real-world tactics in a concise, intuitive way. On the other hand, the promised improvements to the behavior and pathing of computer-controlled players on the field still ring hollow, carrying over many of the same issues the series has had for over a decade. Couple this with the dreaded introduction of open-world elements via The Grounds, and the result is yet another year where nearly positive change is balanced out by a negative one.Ever since NBA 2K14 introduced MyPark, which eventually evolved into The Neighborhood in NBA 2K18 and The City in NBA 2K21, I figured it was only a matter of time before EA brought a similar open world full of activities to its other sports franchises. While The Grounds isn't without merit, it often feels like EA is trying to solve a problem that didn't really exist.

After hours of exploring The Grounds, it’s clear FC 27 didn’t need to have an open-world environment to deliver a more communal online mode. I don’t need to run through a visually saturated, low-resolution city populated by lifeless NPCs just to find a game mode to start up when simple menus devoted to the same function can do that in a more efficient manner. Sure, it works well as an active lobby for matchmaking and makes it easier to find other players and move between activities, but between the framerate drops and unnatural character animations, nothing is immersiveness enough about this hub to justify its existence.

The issues above are only compounded by the myriad of unskippable cutscenes and NBA 2K15-level voice acting that make up The Grounds. The irony is that I was initially excited by the new hub world because it brings back one of my favorite FIFA characters from The Journey story mode: Alex Hunter, who first appeared in FIFA 17 and FIFA 18, once again voiced by Adetomiwa Edun. That enthusiasm disappeared quickly once Hunter began speaking, as his delivery feels noticeably more rigid and detached than it did during his original story.

Edun's performance nearly a decade ago was passionate and natural, whereas The Grounds' version of Hunter sounds like he would rather be anywhere else. Things get even more painful when Kylian Mbappe appears shortly afterward, delivering his lines with such a stiff, mechanical cadence that it was clear he read them directly from the script all in one take. I honestly found myself grateful that my created character doesn't speak to avoid adding even more uncomfortable interactions.

The frustration is only compounded by the constant connection issues and errors that still plague the multiplayer community. From disconnects to server lag, I got kicked from or had to leave more games than I can count in my first full week with FC 27. At one point, I even had a match where my opponent had a goal kick, but instead of kicking the ball, his keeper started floating up the pitch with it. This didn’t end until the poor player was sent back to his home planet like Poochie in The Simpsons. After a few hilarious, confusing seconds, the netminder was able to take his place back between the posts, but I was given a corner kick as a result.

I also played every new minigame, from Mario Kart-like Balloon Ball to Football Tennis. While I had some fun, it wasn’t enough to buck the notion that these elements belong in FIFA Street more than they do FC 27. Combine that with the fact that progression in The Ground is tied to coins and XP that can also be purchased with real money, and it only compounds my worry that the series keeps moving away from the beautiful game I know and love to further push microtransactions.

When it comes to gameplay, FC 27's expanded Tactics system and its effect on gameplay is easily the best addition, wonderfully complementing the playstyles and roles introduced over the past few years by improving strategy, movement, passing, and crossing in numerous ways. Now more than ever, you have more control over how teams behave in different phases of play, going beyond basic formations and instructions by explaining the purpose, strengths, and weaknesses of different tactical approaches.

This becomes particularly useful when building around individual player attributes. As a Manchester United fan, I found that a deeper defensive approach worked especially well for Noussair Mazraoui, whose patient style lets him maintain his position and disrupt attacks without constantly stepping out of shape, while a short-passing buildup gives him chances to use his technical ability without abandoning that defensive structure.

That flexibility became even more apparent when I switched formations on the fly mid-match while playing against Crystal Palace – I found that they were leaving space along the wings, so I moved into a 4-2-2-2, letting Bruno Fernandes operate between the lines and thread passes to a striker such as Benjamin Sesko, creating opportunities for quick combinations and finishes through the middle. Alternatively, when I faced Manchester City, they controlled the wings more successfully. To counter this, I switched to a 4-2-3-1 wide formation, moving Fernandes more centrally so he dictated play and combined with holding midfielders such as Kobbie Mainoo through quick one-two passes.

Separating tactical instructions for possession and defensive phases adds another useful layer, while Player Roles give individual players more specific responsibilities within a formation. Instead of simply placing someone in a position and expecting them to behave a certain way, I could build their role around the specific contribution I wanted from them. For example, if I move into a 4-2-3-1 wide and place Benjamin Šeško on the right side, I can adjust his role depending on the circumstances. As an inside forward, he can cut inward to create shooting opportunities or provide another passing option for Fernandes, while a wider role allows him to stretch the defense and open space through the middle.That same flexibility can be useful defensively, particularly when protecting a lead. If an opponent repeatedly targets his side of the pitch, giving Šeško more defensive responsibility lets him drop back and support the right back, providing another way to protect that flank without abandoning the attacking structure.

What makes the system particularly valuable is that it teaches the strategy behind soccer formations without overwhelming players with unnecessary information. FC 27 does a good job explaining why different shapes work, which players suit them, and how to adjust them against different opponents, making the tactical aspect of the sport approachable while still leaving experienced players plenty of room to experiment.

This is emphasized even more with revamped passing, which now focuses more on manual controls for grounded and lobbed passing, giving more control over where to place the ball and take advantage of the new curved runs. These movements mirror the real-life game smoothly, as the dynamic movement lets a player burst forward into a curved supporting run around defenders rather than a rigid straight line.

While great in theory, these movements can sometimes feel like they work against FC 27’s own computer-controlled behavior. Pathing and defensive logic can still break down on higher difficulties, allowing a carefully constructed gameplan to be undermined by a CPU defender refusing to challenge for a 50/50 ball or making an inexplicable movement. Passing will still occasionally produce similarly frustrating results when a ball aimed toward an open teammate on the right is instead sent toward a covered player in the middle.

To confirm it wasn’t just my mind playing tricks on me, I loaded the skill trainer and was about to see firsthand where I was aiming, thanks to the visual aids it provides. It was beyond frustrating to see how many times I’d set up to pass the ball wide right, left, or center to open space, only for the directional bar on the Skill Trainer to snap back toward the nearest defender in the complete opposite direction of where the reticle should be aiming. Revamped defense had similar linger issues, as defensive backs were still getting fooled or pulled off their spot by opposing runners on counterattacks, resulting in far too many uneven counterattack goals. The series is over 30 annual entries deep at this point, yet it still can’t get vital features like passing down pat.

That said, I was impressed with the improvements to crossing and corner kicks. Both systems produce more convincing positioning battles and give the player greater control inside the box. I scored several successful headers with Harry Maguire from corners during my time with the game, which stood out because I could count on one hand the number of corner routines and headed goals I had scored in previous EA Sports FC entries.

Ultimate Team makes player upgrades much more flexible in FC 27, adding an option to choose between different paths at key stages instead of being locked into a predictable progression. I preferred being able to tailor a player’s PlayStyles and stats to better suit my preferred style of play, and the move toward smaller promo campaigns and a three-PlayStyle+ limit also helps keep special cards from becoming outdated too quickly. While the overall Ultimate Team gameplay and economy balance isn’t drastically different, there are some noticeable issues that clash with some of the revamped systems, specifically for manual goalkeeping and defending.

Manual goalkeeper movement is less responsive than in previous testing builds, especially when reacting to crosses and corners, making a hard position even less attractive to want to play. The move to manual skill from automated defending is great in theory, but defenders are easily exploited by pace-heavy attackers if a single player switch is mistimed. I like that matches yield more coins and higher baseline Season Points (SP), but the value improvement is offset by adjustments to base discard values for lower- and mid-tier gold, silver, and bronze cards that make them less valuable and eliminate helpful trading metas like the Bronze Pack Method.

Career Mode has also received several meaningful upgrades, especially in the transfer market. I felt much more involved, as the process now features staged negotiations, installments, performance bonuses, bidding wars, and rival clubs attempting to hijack deals. My attempt to sign Manu Koné for Manchester United highlighted this perfectly, as he ultimately chose Manchester City despite me agreeing to both the fee and contract.

Player development is also more dynamic in FC 27, with form, fitness, and morale affecting ratings throughout the season, while rivalries, origin stories, starting scenarios, and icon players like Gareth Bale add more variety to Player Career. Unexpected events add further depth through financial penalties, dressing-room conflicts, disciplinary issues, and training-ground incidents, while press conferences now carry greater consequences for morale and squad relationships.

I also appreciated that CPU-controlled clubs finally manage finances and recruitment around their tactical needs, making Career Mode substantially deeper overall. Despite these additions, menus are still slow, animations are recycled each season, and a lot of progression is still tied to the dreadful investment system introduced in EA Sports FC 24.

articles.title: How to Play the Silent Hill Games in Order
articles.body:
Silent Hill has appeared in the restless dreams of horror fans for almost three decades now. The foggy town and its various iterations, plagued by the Otherworld, continue to define the mechanics and ambience of psychological horror to this day.

Each Silent Hill game contains a relatively standalone story, tied to whatever character the Otherworld has decided to bring to its doorstep. However, the lore of Silent Hill develops across games through returning characters as well as memos, posters, and other small details. Despite its fill of contradictions, some of which are only natural for games with multiple endings, there’s a larger story lurking in the background of each protagonist’s path to atonement (or madness).

If the release of Silent Hill: Townfall has sparked your curiosity about how the timeline all fits together, we’ve got you covered.

Approximately 18 Silent Hill games have been released since the franchise debuted in 1999.

Four Silent Hill games were originally developed by Team Silent between 1999 and 2004. Subsequent games, including plenty of spinoffs, were developed by a variety of studios across Japan and North America.

Konami has also published four Silent Hill games for mobile devices: The Orphan trilogy and Silent Hill: The Escape . These have some murky connections to the rest of the franchise. For simplicity’s sake, we are not including these on the full timeline, but there’s still some lore in those for anyone trying to get the full Silent Hill picture.

We also won’t be including the Play Novel , which reimagines the original game, or the interactive streaming series Silent Hill: Ascension .

Which Silent Hill Game Should You Start With?

Where to start is really a matter of what drew you to the series and whether you’re interested in the original gameplay. If you’re looking for a taste of the series on modern consoles, Bloober Team’s Silent Hill 2 remake is a faithful recreation with some quality of life improvements.

If you’re interested in Silent Hill for lore reasons, there’s no harm in starting at the beginning or even with the original Silent Hill 2. Unless you still have a PS1 and can somehow get your hands on an original copy (very cool, if so), your best bet here is looking for emulation guides.

Every Silent Hill Game in Timeline Order

The first four Silent Hill games are considered the “major canon,” with subsequent spin-offs and standalone games making references to the original story, but also creating some contradictions. Some games are directly connected, some loosely reference one another, and others are pretty much entirely their own thing.

Still, we have a rough sense of when these games take place, and it’s up to you how they fit into your understanding of the Otherworld.

The timeline of Silent Hill games actually starts with one of the most recent installments. Silent Hill ƒ takes us to the town of Ebisugaoka in the 1960s, marking the first time the series was set in Japan .

While some loose connections to the lore of the American Silent Hill are revealed through memos and documents, Silent Hill f’s characters, locations , and “version” of the Otherworld are entirely distinct. You play as Hinako, a teenaged girl living in fear of her own future and family, with a unique approach to save states and endings enhanced by writing from Ryukishi07 .

Silent Hill Origins is a prequel that, despite releasing later, directly connects to the original Silent Hill and Silent Hill 3 as part of the “Alessa Gillespie” arc. It also marks the start of some inconsistencies and, despite its direct connection to the mainline games, is debated in its place as canon.

The story, which by in-game logic takes place around the late 70s, follows the truck driving Travis after a crash brings him to Silent Hill. There, he slowly discovers the cult-driven secrets of the town while reckoning with his own traumatic childhood. It’s specifically the “Good” ending from this game that leads into the original Silent Hill, quite literally paving the way for the character of Cheryl.

The original Silent Hill, naturally, stood on its own two feet. It introduced us to the opaque fog that, while serving a practical purpose around real-time generated environments, became the series’ atmospheric staple.

In the late 80s (if you go by Silent Hill 3 logic), a mysterious car crash leads Harry Mason to the eponymous town of Silent Hill. There, he searches for his now missing young daughter, Cheryl, while encountering the original strange cast of characters and nightmares of the Otherworld.

While the canon on this is a bit iffy, we can now think of it as continuing from the “Good” ending of Silent Hill: Origins. And, of course, paving the way for everything else.

Perhaps the best-known game in the series, Silent Hill 2 extends the lore of the town from the first game while introducing new characters and plotlines. And, of course, it gave us the iconic Pyramid Head.

James Sunderland heads to Silent Hill after receiving a letter from his deceased wife saying that’s where he can find her. Art director Masahiro Ito has mentioned the game taking place in the late 70s, but documents in later games peg Silent Hill 2 as taking place about a decade after the original. The 90s timeline slot aligns with the dates we see in a number of diaries, and is thus what we’re going with.

Unlike some of the other games on this list, Silent Hill 2 does not necessarily have a “canon” ending that directly leads to future events.

Now we’re getting into spin-off territory. Silent Hill: The Arcade is particularly unique, focusing more on action shooter mechanics than the eerie psychological horror elements the rest of the series is known for. Still, it’s Silent Hill, and specifically a spin-off game that takes place around the same time as Silent Hill 2.

While it’s generally its own thing, Arcade still offers some interesting insight into earlier Silent Hill history, particularly the sinking of the Little Baroness ship back in 1917.

Yep, things get weird again. The latest Silent Hill game takes place in 1996 on the fictional island of St. Amelia, which places it firmly in the middle of the original Team Silent games.

Protagonist Simon wakes up at the docks of the island with no memory of how he got there. In typical Silent Hill fashion, he quickly encounters some funky characters and his own variation of the Otherworld. These encounters slowly reveal his and the town’s past, and how exactly they’re connected.

Like Silent Hill f, Townfall has looser connections to the initial cult elements of the series, instead staying connected through themes of guilt. And, of course, the joke ending .

While Silent Hill 3 doesn’t technically pick up the story until after Townfall, it most directly follows the events of Silent Hill: Origins and the original game, concluding the aforementioned Alessa arc. Its place on the timeline generally lines up with its own release year in the early 2000s.

The connection here is pretty blatant. You play as Heather, daughter of Harry Mason. The murder of her father (the OG protagonist) prompts Heather to return to Silent Hill 17 years after the first game to learn the true circumstances and implications of her birth.

The last Silent Hill game originally developed by Team Silent carries on from Silent Hill 3 in the early 2000s. One letter in particular clarifies that it’s been a “few years” since the events of the third game.

We’ve since gotten plenty of different iterations of what exactly makes “Silent Hill,” but this was the first game to literally move the game’s location away from the specific town, instead bringing us to Ashfield. There are some character connections to the second and third games, but this one largely stands on its own as you try to help Henry Townsend escape his apartment (and the “Nightmare”).

Homecoming was the first "mainline" Silent Hill game released after Konami disbanded Team Silent. It once again leaves out the actual town of Silent Hill, instead following the protagonist, Alex Shepherd, as he returns to his hometown of Shepherd's Glen.

Homecoming doesn’t have a particularly concrete place on the timeline, but it generally takes place within a few years of The Room. Travis the truck driver makes an appearance, marking a loose connection to Origins, and the game directly addresses the cultish machinations of “The Order” from the original canon.

Downpour is pretty standalone in the grand scheme of things. However, it does bring us back to the actual town of Silent Hill through the classic means of a sad man getting into a car (well, prison transport bus) crash.

There’s not an obvious in-game year attached to the story of Downpour, but general fan consensus places it around the release date of the game itself. Despite its titular setting, there aren’t too many references to the other Silent Hill games, but a certain Pyramid Head does make an appearance. In the joke ending , at least.

Yep, another funky spin-off. This one is particularly distinct, in large part because it’s the one Silent Hill game where you create your own character . It’s also your birthday! And it's a dungeon crawler! Again, a weird one.

In all of its weirdness, though, we do know that Book of Memories takes place very specifically in 2010. Just don’t expect too much insight into the rest of the franchise.

The timeline ends with a recent free-to-play spin-off that followed the cancellation of P.T. and is once again generally its own thing. The Short Message takes place in “modern day” Germany, specifically the small town of Kettenstadt.

Events like the COVID-19 pandemic appear in-game, bringing us into the 2020s. However, the course of the game’s events are heavily influenced by the town’s history back in the 1930s as well as the childhood of its protagonist, Anita.

Sure, it might have been pulled from the PlayStation Store , but P.T. certainly made some waves when it was first released. P.T., which stands for Playable Teaser, was an early demo for the full game of Silent Hills, a collaboration between Konami, Hideo Kojima, and Guillermo del Toro. Unfortunately, the project’s cancellation means we’ll never truly know how it was going to connect to the rest of the series.

Silent Hill fans have had plenty to chew on over the past couple of years with the back-to-back release of Silent Hill ƒ and Silent Hill: Townfall. These were two of the wonkier additions to the full timeline, suggesting Konami’s focus is now on experimenting with what exactly can (and should ) be “Silent Hill”.

While Konami has openly discussed annual Silent Hill releases , we have yet to hear any official announcements about future new games in the franchise. We do know that Bloober Team is following up their Silent Hill 2 remake with a remake of the original 1999 game .

In the meantime, studios continue to take cracks at trying to make a decent Silent Hill movie.

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: Chris Hansen Announces His Own Documentary After Watching 'Fever Dream' Primetime and Grades Movie a D
articles.summary: Chris Hansen says he was more confused than offended by Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime, and is answering this dramatized version of events with his own documentary.
articles.body:
Chris Hansen says he was more confused than offended by Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime, and is answering this dramatized version of events with his own documentary.

Chris Hansen has finally seen Primetime , which he watched in a Times Square theater alongside an audience of average moviegoers — and he says he was more baffled by the film than anything else.

He’s also got “a number of documentaries” about his life and career in the works, one of which is currently being shopped around to multiple different platforms.

Hansen delivered the news during an interview with fellow host and journalist Jesse Watters on his YouTube channel after watching Primetime, where he revealed the documentary’s title: I am Chris Hansen.

“It’s a project, a film, in which I cooperated, produced by folks obviously I know and work with, and it was in the works well before we even heard of Primetime,” he said. “It’s pretty good timing to have this thing out there with our agents shopping it on the West Coast to various platforms.”

Hansen went on to give his review of the movie, which he graded a D. (Hey, at least it wasn’t an F.) And while Hansen praised Robert Pattinson’s performance, he felt the actor’s portrayal of him deviated significantly from who he was as a person — to the point where it was like watching a totally different person on the screen. And that, for Hansen, makes it so separate from his own identity that it’s hard to be offended by it.

“What was in it, in my mind, was something that was so overly-dramatized, so detached from reality — as the director put it, a fever dream — that it almost hit me as something that was so far from reality that it wouldn't even bother me, and I think other filmgoers will experience the same thing.

“In a way, it's a hit piece on me and the series, which is weird, because all we do is expose bad human beings who try to hurt children. So in that respect, it's sort of an insult to the thousands of men and women who want, every day, to do the same thing that I try to do in Takedown and did in To Catch a Predator. It's so far over the top that it's hard to come to grips with what they're trying to do here.”

Hansen went on to mention a specific scene in the film where Pattinson sits in front of a vanity mirror, shirtless, rehearsing what he plans to say to the supposed predators when he gets them on camera. This, like "almost every one” of the other scenes in Primetime, “didn’t happen,” according to Hansen.

Hansen went on to reiterate that he was never approached by A24 about the film. Previously, he claimed that he’d refused to sign a waiver before entering a screening of the movie, alleging that the studio wanted him to “sign away my rights.”

Prior to seeing the film, Hansen slammed it as a “very dramatized version” of events and even purchased advertisements for his own true crime network to air before every single screening of Primetime. In contrast to Hansen’s opinion, we at IGN scored the film a glowing nine out of 10 , calling it a “blast from the past with a sickly allure” that’s “as garish as its subject: Chris Hansen’s To Catch a Predator.”

Image Credits: Mike Pont/WireImage via Getty Images

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .
